title: Reduce sensitivity to pointer movements for the purpose of waking up the screen to prevent unintentional wake-ups
line: A small accidental bump of the mouse no longer turns the screens back on; moving it on purpose still does.
explanation: While the screens are off, KWin's DPMS input filter turned them back on at the first pointer motion event, so even a one-pixel jitter from bumping the desk woke them up. The change makes the filter add up how far the pointer travels in one continuous movement (a pause of more than 500 ms starts over) and only wakes the screens once it has moved at least 50 logical pixels. Keys, clicks, scrolling, touch and tablets wake the screens as before.

commits.message:
dpms: don't wake the screens up when the mouse is barely moved

Any pointer motion turned the screens back on, so bumping the desk or
the mouse a little was enough to wake them up. Now the pointer has to
travel at least 50 pixels without pausing before the screens turn on.

BUG: 384768

media.caption: Master: with the screen off, moving the mouse by 5 px turns it back on
Fixed: several 5 px nudges keep the screen off; a real 250 px movement wakes it

reviews.text: Solid, minimal fix in KWin's DpmsInputEventFilter that requires 50 logical pixels of continuous pointer travel (resetting after a 500 ms pause) before waking outputs, while keeping keys, clicks, scrolling, and touch wake-up unchanged. Falling back from event->delta to position deltas handles both relative devices at screen edges and absolute pointer devices cleanly, and avoiding an unnecessary KCM setting aligns with KDE Plasma UX standards. Updating m_lastPointerPosition on warp events and explicitly including <chrono>/<QPointF> in the header are minor optional cleanups, not blockers.

The KWin DPMS input filter is the right place for this, and the distance threshold (50 logical px within one continuous movement, reset after a 500 ms pause) is sound: warps are skipped, absolute devices are handled, and clicks, keys, scrolling and tablets are unchanged. It only does half the job, though. In PointerInputRedirection::processMotionInternal the spies run before the filters, so UserActivitySpy still reports every small bump as user activity. KIdleTime/ext-idle-notify therefore resume, and PowerDevil's DPMS::onWakeupFromIdle switches the keyboard backlight back on while the screens stay dark; idle timers also restart. The verification used kscreen-doctor --dpms off rather than PowerDevil's idle timeout, so it didn't exercise this path. On a laptop with a backlit keyboard, a desk bump now gives a half-woken machine instead of a dark one.
changes: While the DPMS filter is installed, don't count sub-threshold pointer motion as user activity: e.g. have UserActivitySpy skip pointer motion while outputs are off and have the DPMS filter report the activity itself once the threshold is passed, so the keyboard backlight and idle timers resume only with the screens.

Verify through PowerDevil's real idle DPMS-off timeout on a session with a keyboard backlight (or by watching idle-resume signals): a small bump must neither turn on the screens nor send a resume-from-idle.
Add an integration test (e.g. in outputchanges_test.cpp): with DPMS off, a small relative motion keeps the outputs off and a long motion turns them on.
